samples.text:
In the past, having a good degree or certificate was the most important thing for getting a job. Nowadays, some people say that in the future the ability to learn new skills quickly will be more important than qualifications. I agree with this statement.

The main reason is that technology is changing very fast. Many jobs that exist today will disappear, and new jobs will appear which we cannot imagine now. A person who studied a subject ten years ago may find that his knowledge is already old. For example, many office workers had to learn how to use new software and online tools during the last few years. The people who learned fast was able to keep their job, but others had difficulties. This shows that learning quickly is a very useful ability.

In addition, companies today want employees who can adapt. When a company starts a new project, it need workers who can understand new things without long training. A person with many certificates but who cannot learn is not so helpful for the company. Also, a lot of skills can now be learned online for free, so the qualification from university is not the only way to prove your knowledge.

However, I don't think qualifications will become useless. Some jobs, like doctors, engineers or lawyers, always need official degrees because they are very responsible jobs. Nobody want to be treated by a doctor without a qualification.

In conclusion, I agree that the ability to learn new skills quickly will be more important than qualifications in the future, because the world of work is changing very quickly. But for some professions, qualifications will still be necessary.

samples.text:
It is often claimed that, in the future, the capacity to acquire new skills rapidly will matter more than formal qualifications. I partly agree with this view: adaptability is becoming increasingly valuable in a changing job market, but qualifications will continue to play an essential role, particularly in certain professions.

On the one hand, the pace of technological change means that specific knowledge becomes outdated more quickly than before. Software, industries and even entire job categories can transform within a few years, so employees who can learn new tools and methods efficiently are likely to remain employable. Many employers now place greater emphasis on problem-solving and flexibility during interviews, recognising that a degree obtained years earlier says little about how well a person will cope with tomorrow's challenges. The growth of short online courses also allows workers to update their skills continuously without returning to university.

On the other hand, qualifications still serve important purposes. In fields such as medicine, law and engineering, formal training ensures that professionals meet agreed standards, and it would be dangerous to allow people to practise simply because they claim to learn quickly. Qualifications also provide employers with a reliable way to compare candidates, especially when hundreds of people apply for the same job. Moreover, completing a degree often demonstrate the very ability to learn that critics claim is more important.

In my view, the two are becoming complementary rather than competing. A qualification may open the door to a career, but the ability to keep learning will determine how far a person progresses once they are inside.

In conclusion, I agree that the ability to learn new skills quickly will grow in importance, but I do not think it will replace qualifications. Both will be necessary, with adaptability becoming the key to long-term success.

samples.text:
As automation and digital technology reshape the labour market, many commentators predict that the ability to learn quickly will soon outweigh the value of formal qualifications. I agree with this prediction to a large extent, although I believe qualifications will remain important as a baseline, particularly in regulated professions.

The central argument concerns the shrinking shelf life of knowledge. A graduate entering the workforce today may find that much of what they studied is obsolete within a decade, as new tools, regulations and business models emerge. In such an environment, what distinguishes successful employees is not what they learnt at twenty-two but how effectively they can master unfamiliar tasks at forty. A marketing specialist who can quickly grasp a new analytics platform, for instance, is often more valuable to an employer than a colleague with a more prestigious degree who struggles to adapt.

Hiring practices already reflect this shift. A growing number of companies assess candidates through practical tasks and probation periods rather than relying solely on certificates, and some technology firms have dropped degree requirements for certain roles altogether. At the same time, the availability of online courses and workplace training means that skills can be acquired and demonstrated outside traditional education, weakening the monopoly that formal credentials once held.

Nevertheless, qualifications are unlikely to disappear. In professions where mistakes can endanger lives, such as surgery or civil engineering, society rightly insists on rigorous, standardised training that cannot be replaced by a talent for fast learning. Degrees also signal persistence and a foundation of knowledge on which further learning can be built.

On balance, I expect qualifications to become a starting point rather than a guarantee of career success. Adaptability and the capacity for continuous learning will increasingly determine who thrives, while formal credentials will remain indispensable only where public safety and professional standards demand them.
